title: The JavaScript Event Loop: Why Promise Callbacks Beat setTimeout(0)
objective: Explain how the browser's single JavaScript thread interleaves work through tasks and microtasks, and predict execution order correctly -- including why a promise callback always runs before a setTimeout callback even when the timeout is scheduled first.

content_blocks.heading: One Thread, Many Things to Do
content_blocks.body:
A browser tab runs JavaScript on a single main thread -- the same thread that also handles layout and paint, the mechanics module 4's process/thread content already covered generally, now applied to this one specific, heavily-used thread. Because there's only one thread, JavaScript can't run two pieces of code at the exact same instant; what looks like concurrency (a click handler firing while a fetch is pending, a timer firing while other code runs) is really the browser interleaving separate pieces of work on that one thread, one at a time, run to completion.

The event loop is the mechanism that decides what runs next once the currently-running piece of code finishes -- and the rules it follows for that ordering are precise enough to predict, not arbitrary, even though they can surprise developers who haven't learned them explicitly.

This session covers exactly those rules: two separate queues (tasks and microtasks) with two different draining behaviors, and the practical consequences that follow once you know which queue a given piece of async code actually lands in.

content_blocks.heading: Tasks: Each One Runs to Completion Before the Next Begins
content_blocks.body:
A task is a unit of work the event loop can pick up and run -- the initial script execution, a `setTimeout` callback once its delay elapses, a click handler firing, a network response arriving. Crucially, once a task starts, it runs to completion before the event loop does anything else at all; there's no pausing a task partway through to let a different task sneak in, even if that other task has been waiting.

This is also why a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` doesn't mean "run `fn` immediately" -- it means "schedule a new task for `fn`, to run once the current task finishes and the event loop gets around to it," which could still be after other already-queued tasks, and is never before the currently-running code completes.

User-triggered work (a click, a keypress, a scroll) is also queued as its own task in this same model -- which is why a page can feel unresponsive during a long-running task: the click handler isn't ignored, it's simply waiting its turn in the task queue behind whatever's currently running.

exercises.prompt: A script calls `setTimeout(fn, 0)` and then keeps running synchronous code for another 50ms before finishing. When does `fn` actually run?

options: Only after the current task (the rest of that synchronous code) finishes running to completion first
Immediately, interrupting the synchronous code partway through, since the delay is explicitly set to zero
Before the synchronous code even starts, since setTimeout callbacks are always prioritized ahead of running code
At a random point during the 50ms, depending entirely on how the JavaScript engine happens to schedule it
definition.explanation: A task always runs to completion before the event loop considers anything else -- a zero-millisecond delay doesn't mean immediate execution, it means `fn` is scheduled as a new task that can only run once the currently-executing task (the rest of that synchronous code) has fully finished.

content_blocks.heading: Microtasks: Drained Completely Before the Next Task Starts
content_blocks.body:
Promise `.then()` callbacks don't run as tasks -- they run as microtasks, a separate queue with a different rule: the entire microtask queue is fully drained -- including any new microtasks a microtask itself schedules -- before the event loop moves on to the next task. Jake Archibald's widely-cited post on this exact mechanism walks through the consequence directly: given a resolved promise's `.then()` chained alongside a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` scheduled first, the promise callbacks still run before `fn`, because the microtask queue gets fully emptied at the end of the current task, and only then does the event loop pick up the next task -- which is where the timeout callback is waiting.

This ordering isn't an implementation quirk -- it's deliberate: microtasks are meant for work that should happen immediately after the current synchronous code finishes, before anything else (including rendering) gets a turn, which is exactly the guarantee promise resolution needs to behave predictably.

reference_links.label: Jake Archibald -- Tasks, microtasks, queues and schedules

exercises.prompt: A script schedules `setTimeout(fn, 0)` first, then immediately chains a `.then()` callback onto an already-resolved promise. Which callback actually runs first?

options: The promise's `.then()` callback -- the microtask queue drains completely before the next task (the timeout) can start
The `setTimeout` callback -- tasks always take priority over microtasks regardless of the order they were scheduled in
Whichever one was scheduled first in the code runs first, since both queues process strictly in scheduling order together
Neither runs in any predictable order at all -- this specific execution order is left fully undefined by the language spec
definition.explanation: Microtasks (promise callbacks) are fully drained before the event loop picks up the next task. Even though the setTimeout was scheduled first, its callback becomes a new task that has to wait for the current task to finish and the microtask queue to empty -- which is exactly why the promise callback runs first, a precisely-defined and predictable order, not an accident.

content_blocks.heading: The Gotcha: Microtasks Can Starve the Event Loop Entirely
content_blocks.body:
Because the microtask queue must be fully drained before the next task runs, a microtask that keeps scheduling more microtasks -- a promise chain that resolves into another `.then()`, over and over, recursively -- never lets the event loop move on to the next task at all. A `setTimeout` loop, by contrast, always yields back to the event loop between iterations, since each iteration is its own separate task, giving rendering, input handling, and other pending tasks a chance to run in between.

This means an infinite (or very long) microtask chain can freeze a page far more thoroughly than an equivalent task-based loop would -- not just slowing down other work, but blocking it indefinitely, since the event loop literally cannot reach the next task while microtasks keep refilling the queue ahead of it.

This is a real, documented footgun in async code that recursively chains promises without ever actually waiting on an external task boundary (a timer, a network response) to break the chain -- the recursion feels asynchronous because it's built from promises, but it never actually yields back to the browser at all.

exercises.prompt: A recursive promise chain keeps scheduling a new `.then()` microtask from within each previous one, indefinitely. What's the practical effect on the page, compared to an equivalent `setTimeout`-based loop?

options: It can freeze the page entirely, since the event loop can't reach the next task while microtasks keep refilling the queue
It has no different effect at all -- microtask loops and setTimeout loops behave identically in terms of blocking the page
It actually improves responsiveness, since microtasks are specifically designed to yield to rendering more often than tasks
The browser automatically detects and terminates any microtask chain that would otherwise run for too long without stopping
definition.explanation: Each setTimeout iteration is a separate task, so the event loop gets a chance to handle other pending tasks (rendering, input) between iterations. A recursive microtask chain never lets the event loop move past the current task at all, since the microtask queue must fully drain first -- and if it keeps refilling itself, that never actually happens, freezing the page.

content_blocks.heading: What Task/Microtask Ordering Doesn't Fix: a Genuinely Blocking Synchronous Loop
content_blocks.body:
None of this task/microtask scheduling matters if a single task itself runs a long synchronous loop -- a `for` loop processing a huge array with no `await` or task boundary anywhere inside it blocks the main thread for its entire duration, since a task always runs to completion before anything else (including rendering, including the microtask-vs-task distinction entirely) gets a turn. There's no scheduling trick that interrupts a task partway through; the only fix is breaking the work into multiple smaller tasks (or microtasks, or moving it off the main thread with a Web Worker) so the browser actually gets opportunities to render and respond to input in between chunks.

This is the practical distinction worth keeping straight: task-vs-microtask ordering governs when already-scheduled work runs relative to other already-scheduled work, but it says nothing about how long any single piece of synchronous code is allowed to run once it starts -- that's a separate problem, solved by yielding more often, not by picking a different queue.

exercises.prompt: A single function runs a synchronous loop over a huge array for 3 seconds straight, with no `await` or task boundary inside it. What happens to rendering and user input during those 3 seconds?

options: Both are blocked for the full 3 seconds -- the task runs to completion with no opportunity for anything else to run
Rendering continues normally throughout, since rendering is handled on a separate thread from JavaScript execution entirely
Input events are still processed immediately, even though rendering itself gets delayed until the loop finally finishes
The browser automatically breaks the loop into smaller chunks behind the scenes to keep the page responsive during this time
definition.explanation: A task runs to completion before anything else gets a turn -- rendering, input handling, and every other pending task are all blocked for the loop's entire duration. The only way to avoid this is to break the work into multiple tasks (or move it off the main thread), since no scheduling mechanism interrupts a task once it's already running.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
The browser's single JavaScript thread interleaves work through a precisely-ordered event loop: tasks run to completion one at a time, and the entire microtask queue drains completely between the end of one task and the start of the next -- which is exactly why a promise's `.then()` callback reliably beats a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback, even when the timeout was scheduled first. That same draining rule has a real cost: a self-perpetuating microtask chain can starve the event loop indefinitely, while an equivalent task-based loop always yields in between. None of this scheduling matters, though, against a single long-running synchronous task -- that's blocked thread time no queue ordering can fix.

This session covered subtopic 15.3 specifically; the rendering pipeline itself (HTML parsing, DOM/CSSOM, layout, paint, compositing -- subtopics 15.1 and 15.2) is already covered by this app's existing Critical Rendering Path session. The next session in this module builds on this one directly: browser processes, Web Workers, and the memory model that lets work genuinely move off this one main thread instead of just getting cleverly scheduled on it.
